Input: What do you think will happen to José Abreu in the MLB after being released by the Houston Astros? Jose Abreu was hitting .124 with a 4 OPS+ (that is NOT a typo) when the Astros released him. And that was a very expensive release because it cost the Astros the $30.8 million remaining on Abreu’s guaranteed contract. MLB teams don’t eat that kind of money unless they have no other choice. The Astros eating that much money suggests there is no market for Abreu, at any discount. Because Abreu is relegated to playing first base, DH and pinch hitting — all of which require the ability to hit — it seems unlikely that Abreu will be picked up by a major league team at age 37 and in an apparent downhill spiral. Abreu’s last above-average hitting year was 2022 for the Chicago White Sox, when he hit .304 with a healthy 134 OPS+, but there were signs of a possible decline because the normally dependable 30-homer slugger had only 15 big flies in 679 plate appearances. In his first year with the Astros, Abreu declined precipitously to a .237 average and 87 OPS+ while hitting just 18 homers. But he did manage to drive in 90 runs, so he wasn’t a complete bust. And he upped his hitting game in the postseason, with four homers and 13 RBI in 11 games. That late-season surge had the Astros hoping for a return to form in 2024, but Abreu was sidelined during much of spring training with a knee injury and never regained his timing. Abreu agreed to the unusual step for a grizzled veteran of spending a month in the Minor Leagues. During that period Astros Hall-of-Famer Jeff Bagwell spent time with Abreu in West Palm Beach, FL, trying to help get his swing right and his timing back. But it didn’t pan out, as Bagwell explained: “He went down there and made some adjustments. [Astros assistant hitting coordinator] Rene Rojas spent a lot of time with him. I went down there to see him. I was happy with what I saw. When he came back, it didn’t pan out enough for the organization to see that we could keep trying to see if he could get better, because of the dire need for us to win now. It is a hard decision, because at the end of the day, this is about our ballclub and that’s the only thing that matters, is our ballclub. Four, five, six in the lineup or five, six, whatever, that’s where José needed to hit, and it just didn’t work out. That’s what’s hard is because we still have to find RBIs. That’s the bottom line of trying to win. He helped carry us at the end of last year and into the playoffs and just got behind in Spring Training and never really found it after it,” Bagwell said. “It wasn’t without effort. And when you’re a team that’s struggling like we are to score runs right now, that’s just something out of my control and it’s out of anybody’s control. It’s not like anybody disliked José. He’s a great human being, had a great career. It just didn’t work out and it’s unfortunate for both sides.” When Jeff Bagwell said that Jose Abreu “had” a great career, did he mean that his career is now over? by Michael R. Burch

Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? Everything about the New Testament seems dicey and there are many obvious wild fabrications and bald lies. But it seems likely to me that there is a “real Paul” hidden somewhere behind and beneath all the subterfuge. However, there seems to be no evidence of a “Saul of Tarsus” as a historical person. In his epistles, Paul never mentioned having been known as Saul. Nor did he ever mention any connection with Tarsus. Despite his wide travels in Asia Minor, Paul never mentioned visiting Tarsus. Furthermore, we know the author(s) and/or editor(s) of the book of Acts made things up, such as: The way the author(s) and editor(s) of Acts lied, it’s not hard to imagine one of them made up “Saul of Tarsus” in order to further deceive the gullible. The fact that the famous Jewish historian Flavius Josephus, a religious scholar and scion of an elite rabbinical family who grew up in Jerusalem shortly after the resurrection, knew nothing about the early Christian church, much less the “miracles” of Peter, Paul and the other apostles, casts doubt on everything Acts says. However, someone wrote the Pauline epistles and the “real Paul” seems like the most likely candidate. Paul’s heated disagreements with Peter, James and the Judaizers seem real enough, at least to me. At one point Paul said that he wished the Judaizers would castrate themselves! Why would writers trying to convince the world that Christianity is the “real deal” make up such a dispute? It seems authentic to me. Furthermore, as Dick Hartfield observed: Paul wrote with some modesty a consistent narrative in the first person, in a consistent style and a reasonably consistent theology across seven epistles (Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Philemon, Galatians, Philippians and 1 Thessalonians) still extant. The epistles appear authentic and, in any case, had to have an author and the author may as well be acknowledged as ‘Paul’. Decades after Paul’s death, a number of pseudepigraphical epistles (2 Thessalonians, Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus) were written. The existence of these epistles so close in time to Paul actually argues in favour of Paul’s existence. Why would anyone write a new epistle in the name of someone who supposedly lived recently but whom no one ever met? Thus it seems there were four very different versions of Paul: In conclusion, my educated guess (and it’s just a guess) is that there was a real Paul, albeit with a lot of later adding to and redacting of what he wrote. by Michael R. Does anyone else have problem with meter? I mean, not understanding it. I can force my poems into iambic pentameter, but they just look worse than they looked already. I use a 14 line format with mostly the traditional ABAB, CDCD, EFEF, GHGH with a couplet at the end, but my poems are free verse because they are not in iambic pentameter. Despite being unable to scan poems, I have managed to write metrical poems by ear and have been published by hundreds of literary journals. My poems have been set to music 61 times by 32 composers, so the experts seem to like their musical qualities. My advice is to “hear and imitate” as a singer might a favorite song. Find a poem you like, practice by writing something “similar but different” and you’ll probably find yourself writing meter before long. These are are few of my songs that have been set to music, if you want to use them for practice… Will There Be Starlight by Michael R. Burch Nimrod is best-known today as the Bible’s “mighty hunter before the LORD” who was “a mighty one in the earth.” According to the biblical account, Nimrod was the son of Cush, the grandson of Ham, and the great-grandson of Noah (Genesis 10:8). Cush or Kush is associated with ancient Babylon, so Nimrod has also been associated with Babylon and the famous Tower of Babel. Nimrod is often portrayed as being black or swarthy in complexion. But these are, of course, artists’ imaginings. No one knows if Nimrod really existed, or what he looked like if he did. According to the Bible, Nimrod's kingdom included the cities of Babel/Babylon, Uruk/Erech, Akkad and Calneh, in Shinar, and he also built the Assyrian cities of Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah and Resen: Cush was the father of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the Lord; so it is said, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” His kingdom began in Babylon, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land he went forth into Assyria, where he built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen, which is between Nineveh and the great city of Calah. (Genesis 10:8-12) Nimrod is mentioned in Micah 5:6, which refers to Assyria as “the land of Nimrod,” and in 1 Chronicles 1:10, which includes Nimrod’s name in a genealogy. Nimrod’s prowess as a hunter was such that his skill became proverbial, and the ancients would compliment hunters by saying, “This man is like Nimrod, the greatest hunter in the world.” Nimrod has been associated with the Nephilim, a race of giants called “mighty men” in Genesis 6:4 (KJV). This association has led some to believe that Nimrod was a giant. Many legends sprang up around Nimrod. In Jewish legends, Nimrod was a polytheist who promoted the worship of many gods and thus was the sworn enemy of the monotheist Abraham, whom Nimrod tried to murder (Genesis Rabbah 38:13). Islamic literature also says Nimrod and Abraham battled one other (Qur’an 21:68–70; 37:97–99). Nimrod appears in the mythology of many ancient cultures, including Arabic, Armenian, Greek, Hungarian and Syrian. There is evidence that the Epic of Gilgamesh and the myths of Hercules may have had their origins in myths of Nimrod. In the Recognitions (R 4.29) Nimrod is equated with the legendary Assyrian king Ninus, who appears in the Greek historian Ctesias as the founder of Nineveh. However, in the Homilies (H 9:4-6), Nimrod is equated with Zoroaster. According to Wikipedia, the elusive Nimrod has not been attested in any non-biblical registers, records or king lists. Historians have failed to match Nimrod with any historically attested figure, or to find any historical, linguistic or genetic link between Mesopotamia and the kingdom of Kush, although one suggestion among Mesopotamian figures is Naram-Sin of Akkad, the grandson of the famous King Sargon the Great. The famous Jewish historian Flavius Josephus wrote the following “biography” which we can probably assume to be the Jewish tradition passed down to him: Now it was Nimrod who excited them to such an affront and contempt of God. He was the grandson of Ham, the son of Noah, a bold man, and of great strength of hand. He persuaded them not to ascribe it to God, as if it were through his means they were happy, but to believe that it was their own courage which procured that happiness. He also gradually changed the government into tyranny, seeing no other way of turning men from the fear of God, but to bring them into a constant dependence on his power. He also said he would be revenged on God, if He should have a mind to drown the world again; for that he would build a tower too high for the waters to reach. And that he would avenge himself on God for destroying their forefathers. Now the multitude were very ready to follow the determination of Nimrod, and to esteem it a piece of cowardice to submit to God; and they built a tower, neither sparing any pains, nor being in any degree negligent about the work: and, by reason of the multitude of hands employed in it, it grew very high, sooner than any one could expect; but the thickness of it was so great, and it was so strongly built, that thereby its great height seemed, upon the view, to be less than it really was. It was built of burnt brick, cemented together with mortar, made of bitumen, that it might not be liable to admit water. Can you provide examples of baseball players whose Hall of Fame careers were negatively affected by poor ballparks? These are are Hall of Fame baseball players whose careers were negatively affected by their home ballparks: Joe DiMaggio hit only 41% of his home runs at home. As great as he was, Joltin’ Joe may have been far greater at a friendlier hitting park for right-handed power hitters. Yankee Stadium from 1923 to 1973 was a graveyard for right-handed sluggers, with a left-center power alley up to a mammoth 457 feet deep. As a result, DiMaggio had a 1.016 OPS on the road, and .938 at home, for a difference of -.78. That 1.016 OPS would be sixth all-time among MLB players, and better than Rogers Hornsby, Aaron Judge, Mike Trout, Mickey Mantle and Stan Musial. A good example of the problem DiMaggio faced is his teammate Gil McDougald, who hit only 26% of his home runs at home. McDougald had a 121 tOPS+ on the road, but just 78 at home. That was the hardest time to hit in the history of the toughest park to hit in. Cesar Cedeno and Jim Wynn were also greatly disadvantaged by the cavernous Astrodome dimensions. Conversely, these are the ten HOF players who benefited most from their home ballparks, with the largest career difference in OPS between their home and away splits: Bobby Doerr +.214 Chuck Klein +.214 Hank Greenberg +.210 Larry Walker +.203 Todd Helton +.193 Earl Averill +.163 Ron Santo +.158 Roy Campanella +.157 Wade Boggs +.153 Jimmie Foxx +.150 … Ralph Kiner +.124 Mel Ott +.062 (discussed below) Mickey Mantle +.039 Babe Ruth +0.33 Willie Mays +.022 Hank Aaron +.014 (and just 15 more homers at home) Lou Gehrig -.047 Joe DiMaggio -.078 (just think of Joltin’ Joe in a friendlier home park for righties!) Throughout history, there have been many different gods that have come and gone. Has anyone ever invented a god and then been found out? If so, what was their motive? HUMAN GODS AND GOD-MAKERS by Michael R. Burch There are thousands of “gods” and all of them were invented, from Zeus to Jesus, but in most cases we don’t know the names of the inventors. There are some candidates, however. The first poet we know by name, Enheduanna, elevated her favorite goddess, Inanna, over the pantheon of ancient Sumerian gods. In effect, Enheduanna created the first feminist goddess and she ruled with an iron fingernail! Enheduanna, the daughter of the famous King Sargon the Great of Akkad, is the first ancient writer whose name remains known today. She appears to be the first named poet in human history and the first known author of prayers and hymns. Enheduanna, who lived circa 2285-2250 BCE, is also one of the first women we know by name. Enheduanna revamped her pantheon long before the Yahwist edited the texts of the Hebrew Bible (the Old Testament to Christians) to make his favored god, Yahweh, the supreme god. The Yahwist had his murderous deity replace the more benevolent father-god El (the source of “el” in names like Israel, Michael and Gabriel). First, the Yahwist got rid of Yahweh’s consort, Asherah, in a messy divorce, then his father El, and finally all the other gods completely! It was the Israelite version of Game of Thrones. But the Yahwist was a Johnny-come-lately, as Enheduanna predated him by around 1,700 years! Herodotus, who has been called the “father of history,” said Homer and Hesiod created the ancient Greek gods: It was Hesiod and Homer who first explained to the Greeks the birth of the gods, gave them their names, assigned them their honours and spheres of expertise, and revealed their appearance. So we have four possible early candidates, although in all likelihood someone else created the gods in question and these individuals merely enhanced their reputations (and their own, in the process). Interestingly, Naram-Sin of Akkad, the grandson of King Sargon and thus a relative of Enheduanna, was the first Mesopotamian king known to have claimed divinity for himself, taking the title "God of Akkad." Other human beings who claimed to be gods include Alexander the Great, Yahweh ben Yahweh (Hulon Mitchell, Jr.), and Jesus Christ (if he actually claimed to be god, which I think doubtful). This category would also include Egyptian pharaohs like Ramses I-XI, Roman emperors like Augustus, Chinese emperors beginning with Qin Shi Huang, and Japanese emperors like Hirohito. Imhotep was an ancient Egyptian architect and physician who was elevated to a god two thousand years after his death, becoming the god of medicine and healing. But due to the time gap, we can’t accuse him of deifying himself! Amenhotep was also deified. Romulus and Remus, the legendary founders of Rome, became gods. Many of the alleged “miracles” of Jesus, including dying, being resurrected, appearing to his friends, then ascending into heaven, were performed by Romulus 750 years prior to the purported birth of Jesus. Julius Caesar was defied two years after his death by the Roman senate. All idols with feet of clay, perhaps, but idols nonetheless. by Michael R. Burch

Is there a goddess who controls all other gods? INANNA, THE MOST POWERFUL GODDESS by Michael R. Burch Inanna is the most powerful goddess, thanks to the first poet we know by name, Enheduanna. For it was Enheduanna who elevated Inanna above all the male gods of ancient Mesopotamia. Inanna was the Goddess of love, war, and fertility. Her title was “The Queen of Heaven” and she was also known as (or greatly influenced) Ishtar, Astarte and Aphrodite. Enheduanna may have been the first feminist, or at least the first feminist we know by name. In one of her poems Inanna kills An, the former chief deity in the Mesopotamian pantheon, and thus becomes the supreme leader of the gods. Did Enheduanna "promote" a female deity to the Queen of Heaven? Might this be considered the first feminist poem? Was Enheduanna countermanding the male-dominated society in which she lived, and perhaps even "projecting" her wishes on male rivals? Enheduanna was the daughter of the famous King Sargon the Great of Akkad. She is also the first ancient writer whose name remains known today. She appears to be the first named poet in human history and the first known author of prayers and hymns. Enheduanna, who lived circa 2285-2250 BCE, is also one of the first women we know by name. She was the entu (high priestess) of the goddess Inanna and the moon god Nanna (Sin) in the Sumerian city-state of Ur. Enheduanna's composition Nin-me-šara ("The Exaltation of Inanna"), which I have translated below, details her expulsion from Ur, located in southern Iraq, along with her prayerful request to the goddess for reinstatement. Enheduanna also composed 42 liturgical hymns addressed to temples across Sumer and Akkad. She was also the first editor of a poetry anthology, hymnal or songbook, and the first poet to write in the first person. Her Sumerian Temple Hymns was the first collection of its kind; indeed, Enheduanna so claimed in closing: "My king, something has been created that no one had created before." Today poems and songs are still being assembled via the model she established over 4,000 years ago!
